belongs_to: Two Angles and the Included Side: 'Here are some obvious examples. If the two angles are greater than or equal to a right angle (90 degrees), then it is clear that a triangle is not possible.'
description: Three small drawings side by side in one row, no labels, no numbers. Each drawing is a horizontal base segment at the bottom with one arm rising upward from each end of the base; each arm ends in an open arrowhead (arms are rays that never meet). Drawing 1 (left): both arms lean outward (the left arm leans left, the right arm leans right), so both base angles inside are obtuse (more than 90 degrees); no right-angle marks. Drawing 2 (middle): the left arm is vertical with a small square right-angle mark at the left end of the base (inside, between base and arm); the right arm leans outward to the right (obtuse base angle, no mark). Drawing 3 (right): both arms are vertical (parallel to each other) with a small square right-angle mark at each of the two base ends (2 squares).

belongs_to: Two Angles and the Included Side: 'Now we make one of the base angles an acute angle, say 40 degrees ... (a) Try to find a possible angle B (marked in the figure) for this to happen. (b) What could be smallest value of angle B for the lines to not meet?'
description: A horizontal base segment with A at its left end and B at its right end (labels A and B at the ends, no arrowhead on the base). From A a ray rises up and to the right to a labelled point C at its tip, drawn with an open arrowhead at C; the ray is labelled with the italic letter l along its middle (the line l). A small arc at A between AB and the ray is labelled 40 degrees (written 40°). Nothing is drawn at B: angle B is NOT marked on this figure (the text says 'marked in the figure' but the arc at B appears only in the next page's figure).

belongs_to: Two Angles and the Included Side: 'The blue line is the line with the least rightward bend that doesn't meet the line l.' (the figure follows the 40 degree discussion; leads to angle B = 140 degrees)
description: Same base AB as on the previous page: horizontal segment, A at the left end, B at the right end. From A a ray goes up and to the right to C (open arrowhead at C), labelled l along its middle, with an arc at A labelled 40° (written 40°). From B a fan of 4 rays goes up and to the right, each with an open arrowhead: 1 blue ray (the steepest, drawn highest, parallel in direction to the ray l from A) and 3 black rays, each less steep than the one above it (spread evenly, lowest ray the shallowest). A large arc is drawn at B, starting on the base to the left of B (the BA side) and sweeping over B up to the blue ray: it marks the angle B between BA and the blue ray (obtuse, = 140°, but no number is printed on this arc). Labels shown: A, B, C, l, 40°.

belongs_to: Angle sum / third angle: 'Consider a triangle ABC with angle B = 50° and angle C = 70°. Let us see how we can find angle A without construction.'
description: A triangle with vertex B at the bottom left, C at the bottom right and A at the top (A sits right of the middle of the base, nearer C). Base BC is horizontal. A small arc at B labelled 50° (written 50°) inside the triangle and a small arc at C labelled 70° (written 70°) inside the triangle; no mark or number at A. Vertex labels A, B, C.

belongs_to: Fig. 7.6 - 'Let us suppose we construct a line XY parallel to BC through vertex A. We can see new angles being formed here: angle XAB and angle YAC. What are their values?'
description: The same triangle ABC (B bottom left, C bottom right, A at the top) with a horizontal line XY drawn through A parallel to BC: a filled dot at the left end labelled X, a filled dot at the right end labelled Y, A lies on the line XY between them (the line does not extend beyond the two dots). Arcs: 50° (written 50°) at B inside the triangle, 70° (written 70°) at C inside the triangle, and one small unlabelled arc just below A between AB and AC (the angle BAC). The angles XAB and YAC are not marked. Caption below: 'Fig. 7.6'.

belongs_to: Figure it Out Q3 (angle sum): 'Here is a triangle in which we know angle B = angle C and angle A = 50°. Can you find angle B and angle C?' (Try This)
description: A tall isosceles-looking triangle: A at the top, B at the bottom left, C at the bottom right, base BC horizontal. At A a small arc with the label 50° (written 50°) placed just inside below the arc. At B and at C there is one small arc each, with NO number, drawn with the same single-arc style to show that angle B = angle C. Labels A, B, C.

belongs_to: Angle Sum Property: Fig. 7.7 - the parallel line through A used to prove that angle A + angle B + angle C = 180°
description: A scalene triangle with B at the bottom left, C at the bottom right (base BC horizontal) and A near the top, left of centre. A long horizontal line through A parallel to BC extends beyond both sides; two filled dots on it labelled X (left of A) and Y (right of A); A lies on the line. Coloured angle marks (filled sectors, no numbers): at B a RED sector (angle B); at C a GREEN sector (angle C); at A three sectors side by side along the line: RED on the left between AX and AB (angle XAB, same colour as angle B), BROWN in the middle between AB and AC (angle BAC = angle A), GREEN on the right between AC and AY (angle YAC, same colour as angle C). Caption: 'Fig. 7.7'.

belongs_to: Angle Sum Property: 'There is a convenient way of verifying the angle sum property by folding a triangular cut-out of a paper. Do you see how this shows that the sum of the angles in this triangle is 180°?'
description: Three pictures stacked vertically, all in the same pale tan/cream paper colour with a slight shadow, no labels or numbers. (1) Top: a single large scalene triangle (long base at the bottom, apex at the upper right, nearly a right angle at the top). (2) Middle: the same triangle partly folded: the base is still long; the top corner has been folded down onto the base and the two lower-left and lower-right corners folded in, so the outline is a long low shape with overlapping flaps and fold lines meeting at one point on the base (3 triangular pieces visible). (3) Bottom: the finished fold, a small rectangle (wider than tall) divided by lines into triangular pieces that all meet at one point on its bottom edge, showing the three angles together forming a straight angle.
unclear: Exact fold lines and the number of overlapping triangular flaps in pictures (2) and (3) are small and hard to read; description is approximate for those two.

belongs_to: Exterior Angles: 'The angle formed between the extension of a side of a triangle and the other side is called an exterior angle ... In this figure, angle ACD is an exterior angle.' (used again by the worked example 'Find angle ACD, if angle A = 50°, and angle B = 60°')
description: A triangle with B at the bottom left, A at the top (a little right of the middle of the base), and C at the bottom right end of the triangle. The base BC is extended to the right as a horizontal line from C to a point D marked by a filled dot at its right end. The exterior angle is shown as an arc at C between CA and CD (the angle on the outer side of the triangle), with the text 'Exterior Angle' printed above and to the right of the arc. No degree values. Labels A, B, C, D.

belongs_to: Fig. 7.8 - 'Consider a triangle ABC. What is the height of the vertex A from its opposite side BC ... Let AD be the line segment from A drawn perpendicular to BC.'
description: A triangle with B at the bottom left, C at the bottom right, base BC horizontal and A at the top, close to C (A is above a point near the right end of the base). A vertical segment AD drops from A to a point D on BC (D lies between B and C, closer to C). A small square right-angle mark at D, on the right side of AD (between AD and DC). Labels A, B, C, D. Caption 'Fig. 7.8'. No numbers.

belongs_to: Altitudes: 'The other altitudes are BE and CF in the figure below: the perpendiculars drawn from the other vertices to their respective opposite sides.'
description: A triangle with B at the bottom left, C at the bottom right (base BC horizontal) and A at the top, near the right above C. Two altitudes are drawn inside the triangle, crossing each other: BE from B to a point E on side AC (E is on the right side, in the upper half of AC), with a small square right-angle mark at E; and CF from C to a point F on side AB (F near the top of AB, left of A), with a small square right-angle mark at F. Altitude from A is not drawn. Labels A, B, C, E, F. No numbers.

belongs_to: 'What would the altitude from A to BC be in this triangle?' - 'We extend BC and then drop the perpendicular from A to this line.'
description: Two drawings side by side of the same obtuse-angled triangle ABC: A at the top left, B at the bottom (a little right of A, the obtuse angle is at B), C at the far bottom right, with BC horizontal at the bottom. Left drawing (the question): only the triangle with labels A, B, C. Right drawing (the answer): the same triangle, with side CB extended to the left of B as a DASHED horizontal line ending at a point D, and a DASHED vertical segment AD from A straight down to D (D lies directly below A, to the left of B). Labels A, D, B, C. No right-angle square mark is drawn at D; no numbers.

belongs_to: Construction of the Altitudes of a Triangle - 'Step 1: Keep the ruler aligned to the base. Place the set square on the ruler as shown, such that one of the edges of the right angle touches the ruler.'
description: A teal-green ruler lying horizontally (a long rectangle with long and short tick marks hanging down from its top edge, about 25 ticks, alternating long and short). Standing on the top edge of the ruler at the left is a teal-green set square (a right-angled triangle with a smaller triangular hole cut in it and tiny tick marks along its base and along its vertical edge); its right angle is at its bottom-right, its vertical edge is on the right, and its base lies on the ruler. To the right of the set square, with its base BC resting along the ruler's top edge, is triangle ABC: B at the left (just right of the set square's vertical edge, not overlapping it), C at the right on the ruler edge, A at the top right (above a point near C). Labels A, B, C. The set square has not yet been slid; no altitude drawn.
unclear: Exact tick count on the ruler and set square is an estimate (about 25 on the ruler).

belongs_to: Construction of the Altitudes of a Triangle - 'Step 2: Slide the set square along the ruler till the vertical edge of the set square touches the vertex A.'
description: Same ruler (teal-green, horizontal, ticks hanging down) and same triangle ABC (B at the left and C at the right on the ruler's top edge, A at the top right). The teal-green set square (right-angled triangle with a smaller triangular hole and tick marks on its base and vertical edge) has now been slid to the right along the ruler so that it overlaps the triangle: its vertical edge passes exactly through vertex A (its top corner is at A) and runs straight down to the ruler; its base lies along the ruler; its slanted edge goes from the ruler at lower left up to A. B is to the left of the set square, C to the right of its vertical edge. Labels A, B, C. The altitude line itself is not yet drawn (Step 3 has no picture).
unclear: Exact tick count on the ruler and set square is an estimate.

belongs_to: Right-angled triangles: 'We see that this happens in triangles where one of the angles is a right angle ... Altitude from A to BC' (a side is also an altitude)
description: A right-angled triangle ABC: A at the top, B at the bottom left, C at the bottom right. AB is vertical and BC is horizontal, with a small square right-angle mark inside the triangle at B. AC is the slanted side from A down to C. Labels A, B, C. No numbers. Printed text line above: 'Altitude from A to BC' (here AB itself is the altitude).

belongs_to: Types of Triangles: 'Equilateral triangles have sides of equal length. Isosceles triangles have two sides of equal length. Scalene triangles have sides of three different lengths.' (classification by sides)
description: Three triangles in one row, each with a caption printed below it, no letters and no numbers. (1) 'Equilateral Triangle': an upright triangle with a horizontal base and the apex at the top; one short tick mark across the middle of EACH of its 3 sides (3 tick marks, one per side, showing all sides equal). (2) 'Isosceles Triangle': a tall narrow upright triangle with a horizontal base; one short tick mark across each of the 2 slanted sides (2 tick marks, none on the base) showing the two equal sides. (3) 'Scalene Triangle': a wider triangle with a horizontal base, the top vertex above the left part of the base so the right side is long and slanting; NO tick marks.

belongs_to: Puzzle Time - Shortest Path in a Box!: 'There is a spider in a corner of a box. It wants to reach the farthest opposite corner (marked in the figure) ... walking on the surfaces of the box. What is the shortest path it can take?'
description: A cardboard-looking box (cuboid) drawn in perspective in mustard/gold colour, open on the front side so the inside back, left and floor can be seen. A small black spider sits inside at the lower right, on the floor near the back-right bottom corner. The far opposite corner, the top-left front corner of the box, is marked by several (about 6) short orange spark lines radiating from it. No numbers or measurements. Illustration style (a drawn picture, not a photograph).
unclear: Which exact corner is the spider's corner and which is the marked corner is read from the picture (spider: bottom right inside; marked: top left front); the marking is only the orange sparks.

belongs_to: Puzzle Time - Shortest Path in a Box!: 'Hint:' picture inside a thought bubble (a cartoon spider with a light bulb is thinking)
description: Inside a pale green thought bubble: the same mustard/gold open box standing at the right, with the small black spider inside at the lower right corner on the floor; one face of the box (the left side of the floor, i.e. the left wall) has been folded out flat so a flat mustard rectangle continues the floor of the box to the left in the same plane. Several (about 6) short orange spark lines mark the far end of this flattened piece (the target corner at the left end). The idea shown is unfolding two faces into one flat surface so the path becomes a straight line. No numbers. The cartoon spider with a light bulb at the lower left of the bubble is decoration.
unclear: Which face is folded out (left wall vs. another face) is judged from the picture; number of spark lines (about 6) is approximate in a small picture.

belongs_to: Printed answer of Figure it Out Q1 (book page 150): 'Use the points on the circle and/or the centre to form isosceles triangles. Ans: One such diagram is ... Try more'
description: One circle with a filled dot at its centre. Two more filled dots on the circle, both on the lower part of the circle, close together. Three segments join the three dots: two equal sides from the centre dot down to the two dots on the circle, and a short base segment between the two circle dots (an isosceles triangle with its apex at the centre). A text label 'Centre' sits to the upper right of the circle with an arrow pointing to the centre dot.

belongs_to: Printed answer of Figure it Out Q2 (book page 151), first figure ('A and B are the centres of circles of the same size'): 'Take points C, C1, C2, C3 ... on the circle with centre B ... points D1, D2, D3 ...'
description: Two circles of the same size, overlapping like a Venn diagram, drawn left and right: centre A (dot, label A) of the left circle and centre B (dot, label B) of the right circle, joined by a solid horizontal segment AB; each circle passes through the other's centre. The two circles meet at 2 points: C at the top (dot, label C) and D at the bottom (dot, label D). Solid lines: AC, BC, AD, BD (so triangles ABC and ABD, both equilateral). On the right circle (centre B), 3 more dots to the right of C along the top: C1, C2, C3 (labels with subscripts). 6 DASHED segments: from A to each of C1, C2, C3 (3 dashed lines fanning out from A) and from B to each of C1, C2, C3 (3 dashed lines from B). On the upper-left arc of the left circle (centre A), 3 more dots: D1, D2, D3 (labels with subscripts, D1 nearest to C and D3 furthest left); no segments are drawn to D1, D2, D3.

belongs_to: Printed answer of Figure it Out Q2 (book page 151), second figure ('A, B and C are the centres of circles of the same size'): 'Similarly it can be done for the other figure.'
description: Three circles of the same size overlapping, no segments drawn: a left circle and a right circle side by side at the top, and a third circle below them centred midway; each circle passes through the centres of the other two. Filled dots only at two points: A (at the centre of the left circle) and B (at the centre of the right circle). Letter labels: A and B beside their dots, C at the top where the left and right circles cross, D at the lower crossing point of the left and right circles (which is the centre of the third circle, no dot drawn there).
unclear: The third circle's centre is at D (no dot drawn) and C is the top crossing point; the picture does not show which three points are called the centres, labels are read by position.

belongs_to: Printed answer of Figure it Out Q1 (book page 163): 'For each of the following angles, find another angle for which a triangle is (a) possible, (b) not possible. Find at least two different angles for each category' - the answer is printed as a table
description: A table with a bordered grid: 3 columns (first column unnamed, holding the given angle) and 5 rows (1 header row + 4 data rows). Header row: [blank] | 'Triangle is possible' | 'Triangle is not possible'. Row (a) 30°: possible = 'Another angle should be less than 150°. It could be 50° or 90°. Find the third angle in each case.'; not possible = 'Another angle should be greater than or equal to 150°. It could be 150° or 170°.' Row (b) 70°: possible = 'Another angle should be less than 110°. It could be 60° or 80°. Find the third angle in each case.'; not possible = 'Another angle should be greater than or equal to 110°. It could be 140° or 120°.' Row (c) 54°: possible = 'Another angle should be less than 126°. It could be 90° or 64°. Find the third angle in each case.'; not possible = 'Another angle should be greater than or equal to 126°. It could be 134° or 154°.' Row (d) 144°: possible = 'Another angle should be less than 36°. It could be 20° or 35°. Find the third angle in each case.'; not possible = 'Another angle should be greater than or equal to 36°. It could be 36° or 90°.' The first-column cells read '(a) 30°', '(b) 70°', '(c) 54°', '(d) 144°'. Plain text and numbers only, no colour or shading.
